docs.title: Exploratory Data Analysis — 2026.2
docs.text: Project for Insper's Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning, semester 2026.2, in three deliverables on the same team and datasets: an exploratory data analysis (EDA) and preprocessing pipeline for both a classification and a regression dataset, followed by a neural network built on top of each pipeline.

docs.title: The two analyses
docs.text:
• Classification — UCI Bank Marketing

    Will a client subscribe to a term deposit after a marketing call?

    • 45,211 calls, 16 input features, binary target y
    • Imbalanced: 11.70% yes
    • duration dropped as target leakage
    • Stratified 80/20 split; 51 features after the pipeline

    Start reading · Full report on one page

  • Regression — UCI Seoul Bike Sharing Demand

    How many public bikes are rented in Seoul in a given hour?

    • 8,760 hours, 13 input columns, target rented_bike_count
    • Right-skewed target: train on sqrt(y)
    • Closed hours removed as target leakage
    • Split by whole days, stratified by season; 22 features after the pipeline

    Start reading · Full report on one page

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Both EDA pipelines, built on in the same way: a from-scratch-configured PyTorch MLP, trivial/linear/random-forest baselines, an 8-configuration regularization search, a test set touched exactly once (3 seeds), and error analysis cross-checked against the EDA's own findings.

  • Regression model — bike demand

    A 2-hidden-layer MLP (22 → 64 → 32 → 1) predicting sqrt(rented_bike_count) beats the mandatory linear baseline's test MAE by 53%, and matches an optional random-forest baseline at a fraction of the parameters.

    • Honest negative result: dropout, weight decay and batch norm all hurt validation performance here
    • Error analysis matches the EDA's own top correlates (temperature, hour)

    Read the report

  • Classification model — term deposit subscription

    A 2-hidden-layer MLP (51 → 32 → 16 → 1) beats the mandatory Logistic Regression baseline on every metric, but falls just short of its 15% PR-AUC success criterion and trails an optional random-forest baseline.

    • Honest negative result: only a 6.4% PR-AUC gain over Logistic Regression (criterion: ≥ 15%) — here dropout helps, the opposite of the regression track
    • Error analysis flags a possible data-collection confound (day) the EDA had already warned about

    Read the report

Both EDA reports follow the same stages from the assignment. Each stage is its own page (use the tabs at the top and Next at the bottom of each page), and each report is also available on a single page:

Stage Content 0. Proposal dataset, target, motivation, first risk 1. Initial inspection data dictionary, quality and leakage, target, train/test split 2. Univariate analysis numerical and categorical distributions 3. Bivariate and multivariate analysis correlations, feature vs target, grouped boxplots 4. Preprocessing strategies, PCA / t-SNE / UMAP, Pipeline + ColumnTransformer 5. Synthesis main findings, risks and plan, 10-item summary table

docs.title: Classification or Regression — Bank Marketing (Classification)
docs.text:
Same dataset, task and train/test split as the Classification EDA, same seed (random_state=42) throughout. Its fitted preprocessing Pipeline (code/bank_preprocessing.py) is imported unchanged, carrying forward every one of its decisions: duration dropped as target leakage, "unknown" kept as its own category, the pdays sentinel handled with a missing-indicator, and the stratified 80/20 split.

The team also built the regression track of this same assignment, on the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset from the same EDA — both are submitted; this report covers classification.

Five scripts under code/, run in order from a clean clone:

python3 -m venv env
source ./env/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade
python3 code/classification_baselines.py      # Step 1
python3 code/classification_training.py       # Steps 2-3, Figure 1
python3 code/classification_search.py         # Step 4
python3 code/classification_test_eval.py      # Step 5, Figures 2-3 (touches the test set)
python3 code/classification_error_analysis.py # Step 6

code/classification_common.py and code/classification_model.py hold what every script shares: the inner train/validation split and metrics, and the MLPClassifier + early-stopping training loop, respectively.

docs.title: 0. Starting Point
docs.text:
• Pipeline: bank_preprocessing.build_preprocessor(), fit on the training fold only — unchanged from the EDA (no grading corrections were available for this dataset at the time of writing).
  • Main metric: PR-AUC (average precision) — with an 11.7% positive rate, ROC-AUC and accuracy are both flattering (a model that never predicts "yes" still scores 88.3% accuracy and 0.5 ROC-AUC is the only floor that looks bad); PR-AUC is sensitive to exactly the class that is rare and that the bank cares about (will this client subscribe?).
  • Success criterion, fixed before training: network test PR-AUC at least 15% higher (relative) than Logistic Regression's test PR-AUC. Logistic Regression, not the optional Random Forest, is the mandatory comparison point — Random Forest is reported for context only.
  • Internal validation split: the EDA's 80/20 test split is untouched (test: 9,043 rows); its 80% training side (36,168 rows) is further split, stratified on y, into 30,742 training rows and 5,426 validation rows.

docs.title: 1. Baselines
docs.text:
Three models fit once on the inner training fold, class imbalance handled with class_weight="balanced" (the sklearn equivalent of the network's pos_weight, so every baseline and the network handle the 11.7% positive rate the same way: reweighting the loss/split criterion, not resampling the data):

"""Step 1 - trivial and linear baselines, fit once on the inner training fold
and reused for both the validation report (here) and the test report (Step 5).
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

from classification_common import classification_metrics, fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "outputs"
OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def build_baselines():
    """Dummy (most frequent), linear (balanced LogisticRegression) and an
    optional balanced random forest - all with class_weight="balanced" so the
    11.7% positive rate is handled the same way (loss/split-criterion
    reweighting) the network handles it via pos_weight."""
    return {
        "dummy_most_frequent": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
        "logistic_regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42),
        "random_forest": RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=300, max_depth=12, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    }


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)

    baselines = build_baselines()
    val_results = {}
    for name, model in baselines.items():
        model.fit(Z_train2, y_train2)
        proba = model.predict_proba(Z_val)[:, 1] if hasattr(model, "predict_proba") else model.decision_function(Z_val)
        val_results[name] = classification_metrics(y_val, proba, threshold=0.5)
        print(f"[{name}] validation: pr_auc={val_results[name]['pr_auc']:.4f} "
              f"roc_auc={val_results[name]['roc_auc']:.4f} macro_f1={val_results[name]['macro_f1']:.4f}")

    best_name = max(val_results, key=lambda k: val_results[k]["pr_auc"])
    print(f"\nBest baseline on validation (by PR-AUC): {best_name} -> PR-AUC={val_results[best_name]['pr_auc']:.4f}")

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step1_baselines_val.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({"val_results": val_results, "best_baseline": best_name}, f, indent=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Baseline Validation PR-AUC ROC-AUC Macro F1 Dummy (most frequent) 0.117 0.500 0.469 Logistic Regression (required) 0.415 0.774 0.617 Random Forest (optional) 0.460 0.812 0.679

The dummy baseline's PR-AUC (0.117) is, by construction, exactly the positive rate — the floor any real model must clear. Random Forest already beats Logistic Regression by a wide margin on validation, the first sign (before any network is trained) that this dataset rewards non-linear interactions among the categorical predictors — consistent with the EDA's own finding that poutcome, month and job each carry large, non-monotonic swings in subscription rate.

docs.title: 2. The Network
docs.text:
"""The project's network: a configurable MLP binary classifier.

Output is 1 unit, returning logits (no sigmoid applied inside the model) so
that BCEWithLogitsLoss's fused, numerically-stable log-sigmoid is used, as
required for binary classification. Class imbalance (11.7% positive) is
handled with pos_weight = n_negative / n_positive in the training fold, not
by resampling - it changes the loss's gradient, not the data the network sees,
so validation batches don't need matching treatment.
"""
import copy

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from classification_common import classification_metrics


class MLPClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features: int, hidden_sizes: list, dropout: float = 0.0, batchnorm: bool = False):
        super().__init__()
        layers = []
        in_dim = n_features
        for h in hidden_sizes:
            layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, h))
            if batchnorm:
                layers.append(nn.BatchNorm1d(h))
            layers.append(nn.ReLU())
            if dropout > 0:
                layers.append(nn.Dropout(dropout))
            in_dim = h
        layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, 1))
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).squeeze(-1)  # logits

    def n_params(self) -> int:
        return sum(p.numel() for p in self.parameters())


def train_model(n_features, hidden_sizes, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, *,
                 dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.0,
                 batch_size=256, max_epochs=200, patience=15, seed=42):
    """Adam + BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=...), early stopping on validation
    PR-AUC (threshold-independent, appropriate for 11.7% positive data), best
    weights restored. Returns (model, history)."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = MLPClassifier(n_features, hidden_sizes, dropout=dropout, batchnorm=batchnorm)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)

    n_pos = float(y_train.sum())
    n_neg = float(len(y_train) - n_pos)
    pos_weight = torch.tensor(n_neg / n_pos, dtype=torch.float32)
    loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_weight)

    Xt = torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32)
    yt = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.float32)
    Xv = torch.tensor(X_val, dtype=torch.float32)

    n = Xt.shape[0]
    history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": [], "val_pr_auc": []}
    best_val_pr_auc = -np.inf
    best_state = None
    best_epoch = 0
    epochs_without_improvement = 0
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    val_loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_weight)
    yv_t = torch.tensor(y_val, dtype=torch.float32)

    for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        perm = rng.permutation(n)
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]
            xb, yb = Xt[idx], yt[idx]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            logits = model(xb)
            loss = loss_fn(logits, yb)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item() * len(idx)
        history["train_loss"].append(epoch_loss / n)

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val_logits = model(Xv)
            val_loss = val_loss_fn(val_logits, yv_t).item()
            val_proba = torch.sigmoid(val_logits).numpy()
            val_pr_auc = classification_metrics(y_val, val_proba, threshold=0.5)["pr_auc"]
        history["val_loss"].append(val_loss)
        history["val_pr_auc"].append(val_pr_auc)

        if val_pr_auc > best_val_pr_auc + 1e-6:
            best_val_pr_auc = val_pr_auc
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
            best_epoch = epoch
            epochs_without_improvement = 0
        else:
            epochs_without_improvement += 1
            if epochs_without_improvement >= patience:
                break

    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    history["best_epoch"] = best_epoch
    history["stopped_epoch"] = epoch
    history["best_val_pr_auc"] = best_val_pr_auc
    history["pos_weight"] = float(pos_weight.item())
    return model, history


def predict_proba(model, X) -> np.ndarray:
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32))
        return torch.sigmoid(logits).numpy()

Baseline architecture for Steps 2-3: 51 → 32 → 16 → 1, ReLU hidden activations, 1 linear logit output unit, 2,209 parameters. Layer sizes are arguments, not hard-coded, so Step 4 can sweep them.

  • Widths / depth: 32 then 16, 2 hidden layers — the same mild-taper, two-layer recipe as the regression track, for the same reason: the EDA's categorical drivers interact (e.g. month's effect is itself confounded with contact volume, 1B), which a single wide layer can only approximate by brute force.
  • Activation: ReLU, standard for tabular MLPs, no saturation issue with the standardized/one-hot input block.
  • Initialization: PyTorch's default (Kaiming-uniform, matched to ReLU).
  • Output & loss: 1 linear unit returning a logit (no sigmoid inside the model), trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss — its fused log-sigmoid is numerically stable where a separate Sigmoid + BCELoss can saturate and vanish-gradient on confident logits.
  • Imbalance handling: pos_weight = n_negative / n_positive = 7.549 on the training fold, inside the loss — every false negative on the rare "yes" class costs as much as 7.5 false positives on "no" during training, which is what lets the network find a usable decision boundary at all for an 88%/12% split.
  • Parameters vs. training rows: 2,209 parameters for 30,742 training rows — 13.92 rows per parameter, a considerably more comfortable ratio than the regression track's 4.38, since this dataset has far more rows relative to its (smaller, mostly one-hot) feature count.

docs.title: 3. Training
docs.text:
"""Steps 2-3 - the chosen network architecture, trained once to show
convergence and the overfitting onset (Figure 1: train/val loss curves)."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from classification_common import classification_metrics, fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test
from classification_model import MLPClassifier, predict_proba, train_model

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
FIG_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "figures"
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "outputs"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

HIDDEN_SIZES = [32, 16]
LR = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 256
MAX_EPOCHS = 200
PATIENCE = 15


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)
    n_features = Z_train2.shape[1]

    n_params = MLPClassifier(n_features, HIDDEN_SIZES).n_params()
    print(f"Architecture: {n_features} -> {HIDDEN_SIZES} -> 1, {n_params} parameters")
    print(f"Training rows: {Z_train2.shape[0]} (ratio {Z_train2.shape[0] / n_params:.2f} rows/parameter)")

    model, history = train_model(
        n_features, HIDDEN_SIZES, Z_train2, y_train2.values, Z_val, y_val.values,
        dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False, lr=LR, weight_decay=0.0,
        batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, patience=PATIENCE, seed=42,
    )
    print(f"pos_weight (n_negative/n_positive in training fold): {history['pos_weight']:.4f}")

    val_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_val)
    val_metrics = classification_metrics(y_val, val_proba, threshold=0.5)
    print(f"Stopped at epoch {history['stopped_epoch']}, best epoch {history['best_epoch']}")
    print("Validation metrics (threshold=0.5): " +
          ", ".join(f"{k}={v:.4f}" for k, v in val_metrics.items() if isinstance(v, float)))

    # --- Figure 1: training and validation loss vs epoch ---
    epochs = range(1, len(history["train_loss"]) + 1)
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    ax1.plot(epochs, history["train_loss"], label="Train loss (BCE, pos-weighted)", color="#4C72B0")
    ax1.plot(epochs, history["val_loss"], label="Validation loss (BCE, pos-weighted)", color="#DD8452")
    ax1.axvline(history["best_epoch"], color="green", linestyle="--", alpha=0.6,
                label=f"Best epoch ({history['best_epoch']})")
    ax1.set_title("Figure 1 - Training and validation loss vs. epoch (baseline network)")
    ax1.set_xlabel("Epoch")
    ax1.set_ylabel("Pos-weighted BCE loss")
    ax1.legend()
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig01_loss_curves.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step2_3_baseline_network.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({
            "architecture": f"{n_features}->{HIDDEN_SIZES}->1",
            "n_params": n_params,
            "n_train_rows": int(Z_train2.shape[0]),
            "rows_per_param": Z_train2.shape[0] / n_params,
            "pos_weight": history["pos_weight"],
            "best_epoch": history["best_epoch"],
            "stopped_epoch": history["stopped_epoch"],
            "val_metrics": val_metrics,
            "train_loss_at_best": history["train_loss"][history["best_epoch"] - 1],
            "val_loss_at_best": history["val_loss"][history["best_epoch"] - 1],
            "train_loss_final": history["train_loss"][-1],
            "val_loss_final": history["val_loss"][-1],
        }, f, indent=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
  • Optimizer: Adam, same justification as the regression track (handles the mixed standardized/one-hot feature block without per-group tuning).
  • Learning rate: 1e-3.
  • Batch size: 256 — larger than the regression track's 128, since there are roughly 5.5x more training rows and the positive class (even after pos_weight) needs enough examples per batch to produce a stable gradient.
  • Epochs: capped at 200, early stopping with patience 15 on validation PR-AUC (not loss — PR-AUC is the metric that matters for the imbalance, and the pos-weighted BCE loss is not monotonically related to it), best weights restored.

Convergence and overfitting onset: training loss falls smoothly throughout; validation loss tracks it closely through about epoch 15, then flattens and turns noisy while training loss keeps a slow, steady decline — the onset is milder and arrives much earlier here (epoch ~15 of 37) than in the regression track (epoch ~75 of 284), consistent with this network having a far more comfortable rows-per-parameter ratio. The best validation PR-AUC was reached at epoch 22.

docs.title: 4. Regularization and Hyperparameters
docs.text:
Same recipe as the regression track — dropout, weight decay, batch normalization against the Step 2-3 baseline, plus two widths, 8 configurations, selected on validation PR-AUC:

"""Step 4 - regularization and hyperparameter search: >=2 regularization
techniques (dropout, weight decay, batch normalization) compared against the
Step 2-3 baseline network, plus two architecture widths, all selected on
validation PR-AUC. 8 configurations total."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

from classification_common import classification_metrics, fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test
from classification_model import predict_proba, train_model

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "outputs"
OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

CONFIGS = [
    {"name": "baseline (no reg.)", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.0, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    {"name": "+ dropout 0.2", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.2, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    {"name": "+ weight decay 1e-4", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.0, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 1e-4},
    {"name": "+ dropout 0.2 + weight decay 1e-4", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.2, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 1e-4},
    {"name": "+ batchnorm", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.0, "batchnorm": True, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    {"name": "+ batchnorm + dropout 0.2", "hidden_sizes": [32, 16], "dropout": 0.2, "batchnorm": True, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    {"name": "wider [64, 32] (no reg.)", "hidden_sizes": [64, 32], "dropout": 0.0, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    {"name": "wider [64, 32] + dropout 0.2 + weight decay 1e-4", "hidden_sizes": [64, 32], "dropout": 0.2, "batchnorm": False, "weight_decay": 1e-4},
]

LR = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 256
MAX_EPOCHS = 200
PATIENCE = 15


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)
    n_features = Z_train2.shape[1]

    results = []
    for cfg in CONFIGS:
        model, history = train_model(
            n_features, cfg["hidden_sizes"], Z_train2, y_train2.values, Z_val, y_val.values,
            dropout=cfg["dropout"], batchnorm=cfg["batchnorm"], lr=LR, weight_decay=cfg["weight_decay"],
            batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, patience=PATIENCE, seed=42,
        )
        val_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_val)
        metrics = classification_metrics(y_val, val_proba, threshold=0.5)
        row = {**cfg, "best_epoch": history["best_epoch"], "stopped_epoch": history["stopped_epoch"], **metrics}
        results.append(row)
        print(f"[{cfg['name']}] val_pr_auc={metrics['pr_auc']:.4f} val_roc_auc={metrics['roc_auc']:.4f} "
              f"best_epoch={history['best_epoch']}")

    results.sort(key=lambda r: r["pr_auc"], reverse=True)
    print("\n--- Sorted by validation PR-AUC ---")
    for r in results:
        print(f"{r['name']:<50s} pr_auc={r['pr_auc']:.4f} roc_auc={r['roc_auc']:.4f} macro_f1={r['macro_f1']:.4f}")

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step4_search.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

    best = results[0]
    print(f"\nBest configuration: {best['name']}")
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Configuration Validation PR-AUC ROC-AUC Macro F1 Best epoch + dropout 0.2 0.4688 0.8076 0.6340 72 Wider [64, 32] + dropout 0.2 + weight decay 1e-4 0.4657 0.8027 0.6467 22 + batchnorm + dropout 0.2 0.4652 0.8066 0.6598 31 + dropout 0.2 + weight decay 1e-4 0.4631 0.8063 0.6469 22 Baseline [32, 16] (no reg.) 0.4611 0.8015 0.6488 22 + weight decay 1e-4 0.4586 0.8010 0.6527 22 Wider [64, 32] (no reg.) 0.4567 0.7938 0.6293 20 + batchnorm 0.4561 0.8082 0.6556 9

This is the opposite finding from the regression track, and just as honest a result as that track's negative one. There, every regularization technique hurt; here, dropout helps (0.4688 vs. 0.4611 for the unregularized baseline, +1.7% relative) and trains for over 3x longer before its best epoch (72 vs. 22) — exactly what dropout is supposed to do: slow convergence just enough to keep exploring past the point an unregularized network would already have locked in. The two tracks disagree because their actual overfitting risk differs: 13.92 rows/parameter here versus 4.38 there, and Figure 1 above shows the gap between train and validation loss opening earlier and more persistently here than the regression track's Figure 1 did, despite the far better data-to-parameter ratio — a sign that this task's signal-to-noise ratio (predicting a rare behavioral outcome from mostly weak categorical correlates) is intrinsically harder to fit cleanly than the regression track's smoother, physically-driven target. Weight decay and batch norm, on their own, are roughly neutral to mildly negative (consistent with the regression track), and widening the network without dropout actively hurts (0.4567, worse than the narrow baseline) — more capacity without a way to control it just overfits faster.

Chosen configuration: [32, 16] + dropout 0.2 — carried into Step 5.

docs.title: 5. Test Evaluation
docs.text:
The test set is used exactly once, here. The winning Step 4 configuration is retrained from 3 seeds (42, 43, 44), each with its own validation-chosen, F1-maximizing threshold (the same recipe applied to every baseline too, so precision/recall/F1 are compared fairly — PR-AUC and ROC-AUC do not depend on a threshold at all):

"""Step 5 - the test set, touched exactly once, here. The Step 4 winner is
retrained from 3 different seeds; the classification threshold is chosen on
validation (maximizing F1), BEFORE the test set is looked at, then applied
unchanged to test. Baselines (refit once, deterministic) are evaluated on
test for the same single comparison table. Also produces Figure 2 (ROC) and
Figure 3 (precision-recall curve) from the seed=42 run.
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, roc_curve

from classification_baselines import build_baselines
from classification_common import best_threshold_by_f1, classification_metrics, fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test
from classification_model import predict_proba, train_model

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
FIG_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "figures"
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "outputs"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES = [32, 16]
BEST_DROPOUT = 0.2
BEST_BATCHNORM = False
BEST_WEIGHT_DECAY = 0.0
LR = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 256
MAX_EPOCHS = 200
PATIENCE = 15
SEEDS = [42, 43, 44]

SUCCESS_CRITERION = "Network test PR-AUC at least 15% higher (relative) than Logistic Regression's test PR-AUC"


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)
    Z_test = pre.transform(X_test)
    n_features = Z_train2.shape[1]

    # --- baselines, refit once; threshold also chosen on validation (max F1), same recipe as the network ---
    baselines = build_baselines()
    baseline_test_metrics = {}
    for name, model in baselines.items():
        model.fit(Z_train2, y_train2)
        val_proba = model.predict_proba(Z_val)[:, 1] if hasattr(model, "predict_proba") else model.decision_function(Z_val)
        # the dummy's score is constant, so an F1-optimal threshold is a degenerate,
        # meaningless search; keep it at the conventional 0.5 instead.
        baseline_threshold = 0.5 if name == "dummy_most_frequent" else best_threshold_by_f1(y_val.values, val_proba)
        test_proba = model.predict_proba(Z_test)[:, 1] if hasattr(model, "predict_proba") else model.decision_function(Z_test)
        baseline_test_metrics[name] = classification_metrics(y_test, test_proba, threshold=baseline_threshold)
        print(f"[baseline:{name}] threshold={baseline_threshold:.4f} test pr_auc={baseline_test_metrics[name]['pr_auc']:.4f} "
              f"roc_auc={baseline_test_metrics[name]['roc_auc']:.4f}")

    # --- network, 3 seeds ---
    seed_metrics = []
    seed_models = {}
    chosen_threshold = None
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, history = train_model(
            n_features, BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES, Z_train2, y_train2.values, Z_val, y_val.values,
            dropout=BEST_DROPOUT, batchnorm=BEST_BATCHNORM, lr=LR, weight_decay=BEST_WEIGHT_DECAY,
            batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, patience=PATIENCE, seed=seed,
        )
        val_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_val)
        threshold = best_threshold_by_f1(y_val.values, val_proba)
        if seed == 42:
            chosen_threshold = threshold  # the threshold used in the report's headline table

        test_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_test)
        m = classification_metrics(y_test, test_proba, threshold=threshold)
        m["best_epoch"] = history["best_epoch"]
        seed_metrics.append(m)
        seed_models[seed] = (model, test_proba, threshold)
        print(f"[network seed={seed}] threshold={threshold:.4f} test pr_auc={m['pr_auc']:.4f} "
              f"roc_auc={m['roc_auc']:.4f} macro_f1={m['macro_f1']:.4f}")

    mean_metrics = {k: float(np.mean([m[k] for m in seed_metrics]))
                    for k in ["pr_auc", "roc_auc", "macro_f1", "precision_1", "recall_1", "f1_1"]}
    std_metrics = {k: float(np.std([m[k] for m in seed_metrics]))
                   for k in ["pr_auc", "roc_auc", "macro_f1", "precision_1", "recall_1", "f1_1"]}
    print("\nNetwork test metrics, mean (std) over 3 seeds:")
    for k in mean_metrics:
        print(f"  {k}: {mean_metrics[k]:.4f} ({std_metrics[k]:.4f})")

    logreg_pr_auc = baseline_test_metrics["logistic_regression"]["pr_auc"]
    improvement = (mean_metrics["pr_auc"] - logreg_pr_auc) / logreg_pr_auc
    success = improvement >= 0.15
    print(f"\n{SUCCESS_CRITERION}")
    print(f"LogReg test PR-AUC={logreg_pr_auc:.4f}, network mean test PR-AUC={mean_metrics['pr_auc']:.4f}, "
          f"improvement={improvement * 100:.2f}% -> {'MET' if success else 'NOT MET'}")

    rf_pr_auc = baseline_test_metrics["random_forest"]["pr_auc"]
    print(f"(context only, not the success criterion) vs. random forest test PR-AUC={rf_pr_auc:.4f}: "
          f"network is {'better' if mean_metrics['pr_auc'] > rf_pr_auc else 'worse'}")

    # --- Figures 2 & 3, seed=42 run ---
    model_42, test_proba_42, thr_42 = seed_models[42]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, test_proba_42)
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, test_proba_42)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color="#4C72B0", label=f"Network (AUC={seed_metrics[0]['roc_auc']:.3f})")
    plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", linewidth=1, label="Chance")
    plt.title("Figure 2 - ROC curve, test set (seed=42)")
    plt.xlabel("False positive rate")
    plt.ylabel("True positive rate")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig02_roc_curve.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close()

    plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
    plt.plot(recall, precision, color="#DD8452", label=f"Network (AP={seed_metrics[0]['pr_auc']:.3f})")
    plt.axhline(y_test.mean(), color="k", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label=f"Chance (positive rate={y_test.mean():.3f})")
    plt.title("Figure 3 - Precision-recall curve, test set (seed=42)")
    plt.xlabel("Recall")
    plt.ylabel("Precision")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig03_pr_curve.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close()

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step5_test_eval.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({
            "baseline_test_metrics": baseline_test_metrics,
            "seed_metrics": seed_metrics,
            "mean_metrics": mean_metrics,
            "std_metrics": std_metrics,
            "chosen_threshold_seed42": chosen_threshold,
            "success_criterion": SUCCESS_CRITERION,
            "logreg_pr_auc": logreg_pr_auc,
            "improvement_pct": improvement * 100,
            "success": success,
        }, f, indent=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Model Threshold Test PR-AUC ROC-AUC Precision (yes) Recall (yes) F1 (yes) Macro F1 Dummy (most frequent) 0.500 0.117 0.500 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.469 Logistic Regression (required) 0.644 0.409 0.772 0.453 0.440 0.447 0.687 Random Forest (optional) 0.556 0.443 0.799 0.410 0.539 0.466 0.691 Network (mean ± std, 3 seeds) ~0.69 0.435 ± 0.003 0.794 ± 0.001 0.472 ± 0.011 0.499 ± 0.012 0.485 ± 0.004 0.707 ± 0.002

Success criterion: network test PR-AUC at least 15% higher (relative) than Logistic Regression's. LogReg: 0.4091; network: 0.4352 — a 6.4% relative improvement. Criterion NOT met. This is the honest negative result for this track (mirroring the regression track's honest negative result in Step 4, the other direction): the network is measurably better than the required linear baseline, and has the best macro F1 of any model here (0.707, ahead of Random Forest's 0.691), but the margin over Logistic Regression is real without being large, and the network's own test PR-AUC (0.435) sits slightly below the optional Random Forest baseline's (0.443) — the one case across both tracks where an ensemble of trees beats the hand-built network outright.

Figure 2's ROC curve (AUC 0.794) and Figure 3's PR curve (AP 0.435, well above the 0.117 chance line, peaking around 0.75 precision near 10% recall before falling off) both show a model with genuine, well-calibrated-looking discriminative power — this is not a near-random result, just a modest one relative to the 15% bar. The gap between macro F1 (where the network wins) and PR-AUC (where Random Forest edges ahead) says something specific: at its own chosen operating threshold, the network balances precision and recall on the "yes" class slightly better than the trees do, but Random Forest's probability ranking is marginally better calibrated across every possible threshold (what PR-AUC measures) — the kind of distinction that would matter if the bank later wants to change its calling budget (and hence its threshold) without retraining.

docs.title: 6. Error Analysis
docs.text:
"""Step 6 - error analysis: error per subgroup (poutcome, month, job - the
EDA's own three strongest categorical drivers, 55.4/44.2/21.6 pp subscription-
rate spread respectively), the worst examples with hypotheses, and permutation
importance compared against those EDA findings.
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from classification_common import best_threshold_by_f1, classification_metrics, fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test
from classification_model import MLPClassifier, predict_proba, train_model

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "classification" / "outputs"

BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES = [32, 16]
BEST_DROPOUT = 0.2
LR = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 256
MAX_EPOCHS = 200
PATIENCE = 15
N_PERMUTATIONS = 10


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)
    Z_test = pre.transform(X_test)
    n_features = Z_train2.shape[1]
    feature_names = pre.get_feature_names_out()

    model, _ = train_model(
        n_features, BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES, Z_train2, y_train2.values, Z_val, y_val.values,
        dropout=BEST_DROPOUT, batchnorm=False, lr=LR, weight_decay=0.0,
        batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, patience=PATIENCE, seed=42,
    )
    val_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_val)
    threshold = best_threshold_by_f1(y_val.values, val_proba)
    test_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_test)
    test_pred = (test_proba >= threshold).astype(int)
    print(f"Threshold (max F1 on validation): {threshold:.4f}")

    # --- subgroup errors ---
    meta = X_test.reset_index(drop=True).copy()
    meta["actual"] = y_test.values
    meta["proba"] = test_proba
    meta["pred"] = test_pred
    meta["correct"] = meta["actual"] == meta["pred"]
    meta["error_type"] = np.select(
        [(~meta["correct"]) & (meta["actual"] == 1), (~meta["correct"]) & (meta["actual"] == 0)],
        ["false_negative", "false_positive"], default="correct")

    subgroup_rows = []
    for col in ["poutcome", "month", "job"]:
        for level, group in meta.groupby(col):
            subgroup_rows.append({
                "group_col": col, "level": level, "n": len(group),
                "error_rate": float((~group["correct"]).mean()),
                "actual_positive_rate": float(group["actual"].mean()),
                "recall_1": float(group.loc[group["actual"] == 1, "pred"].mean()) if (group["actual"] == 1).any() else None,
            })
    subgroup_df = pd.DataFrame(subgroup_rows).sort_values("error_rate", ascending=False)
    print("\n--- Subgroup error rate (sorted, worst first, top 15) ---")
    print(subgroup_df.head(15).to_string(index=False))

    # --- worst (most confident wrong) examples ---
    meta["confidence"] = np.where(meta["pred"] == 1, meta["proba"], 1 - meta["proba"])
    worst = meta[~meta["correct"]].sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).head(10)
    worst_cols = ["poutcome", "month", "job", "actual", "pred", "proba", "error_type"]
    print("\n--- 10 most confident wrong predictions ---")
    print(worst[worst_cols].to_string(index=False))

    # --- permutation importance (manual: shuffle each preprocessed column, measure PR-AUC drop) ---
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    base_pr_auc = classification_metrics(y_test, test_proba, threshold)["pr_auc"]
    importances = {}
    for j, name in enumerate(feature_names):
        decreases = []
        for _ in range(N_PERMUTATIONS):
            Z_perm = Z_test.copy()
            Z_perm[:, j] = rng.permutation(Z_perm[:, j])
            perm_proba = predict_proba(model, Z_perm)
            perm_pr_auc = classification_metrics(y_test, perm_proba, threshold)["pr_auc"]
            decreases.append(base_pr_auc - perm_pr_auc)
        importances[name] = float(np.mean(decreases))

    importance_series = pd.Series(importances).sort_values(ascending=False)
    print("\n--- Permutation importance (PR-AUC drop when shuffled, top 12) ---")
    print(importance_series.head(12).to_string())

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step6_error_analysis.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({
            "threshold": threshold,
            "subgroups": subgroup_df.to_dict(orient="records"),
            "worst_examples": worst[worst_cols].to_dict(orient="records"),
            "permutation_importance": importance_series.to_dict(),
            "base_test_pr_auc": base_pr_auc,
        }, f, indent=2, default=str)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Error rate by subgroup, for the three categorical features the EDA ranked as the strongest drivers of subscription rate (poutcome: 55.4 pp spread; month: 44.2 pp; job: 21.6 pp):

Subgroup n (test) Error rate Actual positive rate month = mar 86 46.5% 57.0% month = oct 146 44.5% 43.8% month = sep 128 43.8% 50.8% month = dec 36 38.9% 44.4% poutcome = success 306 33.3% 65.0% job = student 180 32.8% 27.8% job = retired 452 26.8% 22.1%

The four worst months (mar, oct, sep, dec) are exactly the four thinnest months in the EDA's own cardinality table (training counts of a few hundred each, versus May's 30.6% share of all contacts) — the EDA already flagged these as having "wide confidence intervals" on their subscription rate precisely because so few examples exist. The network inherits that same statistical thinness: it cannot learn a reliable month-specific pattern for sep/oct/mar/dec from a few hundred training examples apiece, so its errors concentrate exactly where the EDA predicted the data itself would be least informative — a direct validation of the EDA's own caution, now showing up as a modelling consequence rather than just a confidence-interval width.

poutcome = success is a different, more interesting failure mode: this is the single strongest individual predictor the EDA found (65% actual subscription rate here, vs. 9-16% for the other three levels), yet it has the third-highest error rate (33.3%). The ten most confident wrong predictions make the mechanism explicit:

poutcome month job actual predicted proba success dec services 0 (no) 0.991 success sep retired 0 (no) 0.990 success sep admin. 0 (no) 0.988 success feb student 0 (no) 0.987 success feb student 0 (no) 0.985 success sep admin. 0 (no) 0.985 success jun student 0 (no) 0.984

Nine of the ten most confident wrong predictions are false positives on poutcome = success clients who still said no. The network (correctly) learned that poutcome = success is an extremely strong positive signal — but "extremely strong" is still only 65% in the data, not 100%, and the network's confidence (consistently > 0.98) overshoots what that signal actually guarantees. This is a calibration problem on the single most important feature, not a case of the network missing the signal.

Permutation importance (PR-AUC drop when a feature is shuffled, mean over 10 permutations):

Feature PR-AUC drop day 0.0577 poutcome_success 0.0520 contact_unknown 0.0424 month_feb 0.0171 previous 0.0135 poutcome_failure 0.0122

poutcome_success and contact_unknown ranking highly matches the EDA directly: poutcome was its single strongest categorical driver (55.4 pp spread), and contact = "unknown" was flagged as having its own distinct subscription rate (4.07% vs. 14.78% when known) tied to a recording-practice artifact concentrated in the first 30% of the file by row order. day ranking first is the one genuinely concerning finding here, not a confirmation. The EDA explicitly described day as reflecting "call scheduling rather than a smooth quantity" and flagged a broader row-order drift linked to the data's collection period (no year column; contact = unknown is concentrated early in the file). day's outsized importance is plausible evidence that the network is partly exploiting that same scheduling/collection-period confound rather than a stable, causal relationship between calendar day and a client's propensity to subscribe — a risk the EDA warned about for exactly this kind of feature, and one future work should test directly (Step 7).

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
Was the network worthwhile? Partially. It clears the required Logistic Regression baseline on every single metric reported (PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, macro F1), and has the best macro F1 of the four models compared — but the 15% relative PR-AUC improvement set in Step 0 was not met (6.4% achieved), and on the metric that mattered most for Step 0's own reasoning (PR-AUC, chosen for the class imbalance), the simpler, un-tuned Random Forest baseline is marginally ahead. For this dataset, a from-scratch 2-hidden-layer MLP is a real but modest improvement over a linear model, not a clear win over a well-understood tree ensemble.

Limitations: (1) the day permutation-importance finding (Step 6) suggests part of the network's predictive power may rest on a data-collection artifact (scheduling/row-order drift) the EDA flagged, rather than a genuinely causal signal — this limits how much the reported test performance should be trusted to transfer to a future, differently-scheduled campaign. (2) The thin-month subgroups (mar, sep, oct, dec) are both the worst-performing and the least-tested (dozens to ~150 test rows each) — the error-rate estimates for those months carry real sampling uncertainty on top of the genuine difficulty. (3) The poutcome = success overconfidence (Step 6) means the network's probability outputs are not well calibrated on its single strongest feature, which matters if the bank wants to use the raw probability (not just the yes/no call) to prioritize which clients to call first.

Affected stakeholders: the marketing/call-center team deciding whom to contact. The calibration issue on poutcome = success is directly actionable: if call-center capacity is limited and clients are prioritized by predicted probability, the current network would over-rank "previously successful" clients relative to their true 65% conversion rate, potentially crowding out other, better-calibrated-but-lower-raw-probability leads from other segments.

Future work: (1) directly test the day/row-order-drift hypothesis by re-running Step 6's permutation importance with day and contact removed, to see whether the remaining features alone still clear the success criterion, or whether performance was partly inflated by the confound. (2) Probability calibration (e.g. Platt scaling or isotonic regression) fit on the validation set, specifically targeting the poutcome = success overconfidence. (3) A log-odds or hierarchical treatment of month, pooling the thin months (mar, sep, oct, dec) toward a shared estimate instead of letting the network fit each in isolation from only a few hundred examples.

docs.title: Classification or Regression — Seoul Bike Sharing Demand (Regression)
docs.text:
Same dataset, task and train/test split as the Regression EDA, same seed (random_state=42) throughout. No model was trained in the EDA; this report picks up exactly where it left off: its fitted preprocessing Pipeline (code/bike_preprocessing.py) is imported unchanged, and every one of its risk-mitigation decisions (grouped-by-day split, sqrt(y) target transform, dropping functioning_day/dew_point) is carried forward rather than re-derived.

Five scripts under code/, run in order from a clean clone:

python3 -m venv env
source ./env/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade
python3 code/regression_baselines.py      # Step 1
python3 code/regression_training.py       # Steps 2-3, Figure 1
python3 code/regression_search.py         # Step 4
python3 code/regression_test_eval.py      # Step 5, Figures 2-3 (touches the test set)
python3 code/regression_error_analysis.py # Step 6

code/regression_common.py and code/regression_model.py hold what every script shares: the inner train/validation split and metrics, and the MLPRegressor + early-stopping training loop, respectively. All numbers below are also saved as JSON under docs/projects/regression/outputs/.

docs.title: 0. Starting Point
docs.text:
• Pipeline: bike_preprocessing.build_preprocessor(), fit on the training fold only — unchanged from the EDA (no grading corrections were available for this dataset at the time of writing).
  • Main metric: MAE, in bikes/hour — the unit stakeholders (fleet rebalancing staff) reason in directly, and more robust than RMSE to the handful of very-high-demand outlier hours the EDA already flagged (Figure 1 of the EDA, skewness 1.125).
  • Success criterion, fixed before training: network test MAE at least 15% lower than the Ridge (linear) baseline's test MAE. Ridge rather than the optional Random Forest baseline, because Ridge is the mandatory comparison point for "does a network learn something a linear model cannot" — Random Forest is reported too, for context, but clearing it was never the bar.
  • Internal validation split: the EDA's 80/20 test split is untouched; its 80% training side is further split 1-in-6 (StratifiedGroupKFold, grouped by date, stratified by season, same recipe the EDA used for the outer split) into 5,609 training rows (235 days) and 1,152 validation rows (47 days) — never mixing hours from the same day across the split, per the EDA's risk #1.

docs.title: 1. Baselines
docs.text:
Three models, all trained on sqrt(y) via TransformedTargetRegressor (the same target transform the network uses below, so every comparison in this report is apples-to-apples), fit once on the inner training fold and evaluated on validation here:

"""Step 1 - trivial and linear baselines, fit once on the inner training fold
and reused for both the validation report (here) and the test report (Step 5).
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

from regression_common import fit_pipeline, load_train_val_test, regression_metrics, sqrt_inverse, sqrt_transform

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "regression" / "outputs"
OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def build_baselines():
    """Dummy (mean), linear (Ridge) and an optional random forest, all trained
    on sqrt(y) via TransformedTargetRegressor - the same target transform the
    network uses, so the comparison in Step 5 is apples-to-apples."""
    return {
        "dummy_mean": TransformedTargetRegressor(
            regressor=DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"), func=sqrt_transform, inverse_func=sqrt_inverse),
        "ridge": TransformedTargetRegressor(
            regressor=Ridge(alpha=1.0, random_state=42), func=sqrt_transform, inverse_func=sqrt_inverse),
        "random_forest": TransformedTargetRegressor(
            regressor=RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=12, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
            func=sqrt_transform, inverse_func=sqrt_inverse),
    }


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)

    baselines = build_baselines()
    val_results = {}
    for name, model in baselines.items():
        model.fit(Z_train2, y_train2)
        pred = model.predict(Z_val)
        val_results[name] = regression_metrics(y_val, pred)
        print(f"[{name}] validation: " + ", ".join(f"{k}={v:.4f}" for k, v in val_results[name].items()))

    best_name = min(val_results, key=lambda k: val_results[k]["mae"])
    print(f"\nBest baseline on validation (by MAE): {best_name} -> MAE={val_results[best_name]['mae']:.4f}")

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step1_baselines_val.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({"val_results": val_results, "best_baseline": best_name}, f, indent=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.text:
"""The project's network: a configurable MLP regressor trained on sqrt(rented_bike_count),
with early stopping on validation RMSE (original scale), restoring the best weights.
"""
import copy

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from regression_common import regression_metrics, sqrt_inverse


class MLPRegressor(nn.Module):
    """1 linear output unit; sqrt-scale target, trained with MSE on that scale."""

    def __init__(self, n_features: int, hidden_sizes: list, dropout: float = 0.0, batchnorm: bool = False):
        super().__init__()
        layers = []
        in_dim = n_features
        for h in hidden_sizes:
            layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, h))
            if batchnorm:
                layers.append(nn.BatchNorm1d(h))
            layers.append(nn.ReLU())
            if dropout > 0:
                layers.append(nn.Dropout(dropout))
            in_dim = h
        layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, 1))
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).squeeze(-1)

    def n_params(self) -> int:
        return sum(p.numel() for p in self.parameters())


def train_model(n_features, hidden_sizes, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, *,
                 dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.0,
                 batch_size=128, max_epochs=300, patience=20, seed=42):
    """Full training loop: Adam, early stopping on validation RMSE (original
    scale), best weights restored. Returns (model, history) where history has
    per-epoch train/val loss (sqrt-scale MSE) and val RMSE (original scale)."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = MLPRegressor(n_features, hidden_sizes, dropout=dropout, batchnorm=batchnorm)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

    Xt = torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32)
    yt = torch.tensor(np.sqrt(y_train), dtype=torch.float32)
    Xv = torch.tensor(X_val, dtype=torch.float32)
    yv_sqrt = torch.tensor(np.sqrt(y_val), dtype=torch.float32)

    n = Xt.shape[0]
    history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": [], "val_rmse": []}
    best_val_rmse = np.inf
    best_state = None
    best_epoch = 0
    epochs_without_improvement = 0
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        perm = rng.permutation(n)
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]
            xb, yb = Xt[idx], yt[idx]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            pred = model(xb)
            loss = loss_fn(pred, yb)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item() * len(idx)
        history["train_loss"].append(epoch_loss / n)

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val_pred_sqrt = model(Xv)
            val_loss = loss_fn(val_pred_sqrt, yv_sqrt).item()
            val_rmse = regression_metrics(y_val, sqrt_inverse(val_pred_sqrt.numpy()))["rmse"]
        history["val_loss"].append(val_loss)
        history["val_rmse"].append(val_rmse)

        if val_rmse < best_val_rmse - 1e-6:
            best_val_rmse = val_rmse
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
            best_epoch = epoch
            epochs_without_improvement = 0
        else:
            epochs_without_improvement += 1
            if epochs_without_improvement >= patience:
                break

    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    history["best_epoch"] = best_epoch
    history["stopped_epoch"] = epoch
    history["best_val_rmse"] = best_val_rmse
    return model, history


def predict(model, X) -> np.ndarray:
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred_sqrt = model(torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()
    return sqrt_inverse(pred_sqrt)

Baseline architecture for Steps 2-3: 22 → 32 → 16 → 1, ReLU hidden activations, 1 linear output unit (predicting sqrt(rented_bike_count)), 1,281 parameters. Layer sizes are arguments to MLPRegressor, not hard-coded, so Step 4 can sweep them.

  • Widths: 32 then 16 — halving each layer is a standard, mild taper; justified relative to data size below.
  • Depth: 2 hidden layers — the EDA's PCA needed 7 components for 80% of the variance and flagged genuine season→precipitation→hour interactions (non-additive effects), which a single hidden layer can approximate only by brute-force width; two layers let the network compose "is it a commuter hour" with "is the weather good" more cheaply.
  • Activation: ReLU — unlike tanh (used for the exercises), it does not saturate for the wide numeric range StandardScaler outputs still carry after the EDA's clipping, and is the standard default for tabular MLPs.
  • Initialization: PyTorch's default (Kaiming-uniform for Linear, matched to ReLU) — no custom scheme was needed; training converges cleanly (Figure 1).
  • Output & loss: 1 linear unit, MSELoss on sqrt(rented_bike_count) — not raw counts. The EDA measured the raw target's skewness at 1.125 and found sqrt (0.352) beats log1p (-0.749, overcorrects) as a variance-stabilizing transform (its own risk #2); squaring the prediction back (always ≥ 0, no clipping needed) is exactly TransformedTargetRegressor's recipe, applied here by hand since the model is a torch network, not an sklearn estimator.
  • Parameters vs. training rows: 1,281 parameters for 5,609 training rows — 4.38 rows per parameter. Comfortable for a shallow MLP on standardized tabular features, and Step 4 checks whether a wider network (fewer rows/parameter) still generalizes once regularization is accounted for.

  • Learning rate: 1e-3 (Adam's standard default) — the loss curve (Figure 1) drops smoothly with no oscillation, so this was not tuned further.
  • Batch size: 128 — small enough for frequent updates on ~5,600 rows (44 batches/epoch), large enough to keep per-batch gradient noise reasonable.
  • Epochs: capped at 300, early stopping with patience 20 on validation RMSE (original bikes/hour scale, not the sqrt-scale training loss), best weights restored.

Convergence and overfitting onset: both curves fall together through about epoch 75 (log scale needed to see this — the initial drop from ~700 to ~20 in the first 5 epochs would otherwise hide everything after it). Past epoch ~75-100 the training loss keeps falling (8.18 at the final epoch) while validation plateaus and turns noisy (11.88 final, but its minimum, 12.17, was already reached at epoch 264) — a textbook, if modest, overfitting onset: the gap between train and validation loss is real but small, which is why early stopping alone (no explicit regularizer) turns out to be enough, as Step 4 confirms.

retrained from 3 different seeds (on train+val refit of the preprocessor is
NOT redone - the pipeline and the inner train/val split stay exactly as in
Steps 1-4; only the network's own weight-init/shuffle seed varies), and its
mean +/- std test metrics are compared against the baselines (refit once,

        json.dump({
            "baseline_test_metrics": baseline_test_metrics,
            "seed_metrics": seed_metrics,
            "mean_metrics": mean_metrics,
            "std_metrics": std_metrics,

Success criterion: network test MAE at least 15% lower than Ridge's. Ridge: 281.28; network: 131.55 — a 53.2% reduction. Criterion met, by a wide margin. For context only (not the success criterion, decided in Step 0 before the network ever saw the test set): the network's mean test MAE (131.55) also edges out the optional Random Forest baseline (133.77) — a genuinely strong result for a ~3,600-parameter network against an ensemble of 300 trees, though the two are close enough (within the network's own seed-to-seed std of 3.07) that this particular edge should not be over-read.

MAPE is reported but is the least trustworthy of the four metrics here: the target's minimum is 2 (never exactly 0, so it is computable), but 0.46% of all rows have y < 10, and a modest absolute error on one of those hours produces a huge relative error — exactly the kind of instability visible in its larger std (4.97 points) relative to its own mean, compared to MAE's tighter std (3.07 on a mean of 131.55).

Figure 2 shows the fit is tight and follows the diagonal well up to roughly 2,500 bikes/hour, with a slight tendency to under-predict the very highest-demand hours (the handful of points below the diagonal past 2,500). Figure 3's funnel shape — residual spread growing with predicted demand — is the same heteroscedasticity the EDA flagged (its Figure 7: winter's spread is much narrower than summer's); sqrt(y) reduces but does not eliminate it, since the variance-stabilizing property of sqrt is only exact for Poisson-like counts, and real demand is over-dispersed relative to that at high-traffic hours.

OUT_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "projects" / "regression" / "outputs"

BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES = [64, 32]
LR = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 128
MAX_EPOCHS = 300
PATIENCE = 20
N_PERMUTATIONS = 20


def precipitation_regime(row):
    if row["rainfall"] > 0:
        return "rain"
    if row["snowfall"] > 0:
        return "snow"
    return "dry"


def main():
    X_train2, X_val, X_test, y_train2, y_val, y_test, X_train, y_train = load_train_val_test()
    pre = fit_pipeline(X_train2)
    Z_train2 = pre.transform(X_train2)
    Z_val = pre.transform(X_val)
    Z_test = pre.transform(X_test)
    n_features = Z_train2.shape[1]
    feature_names = pre.get_feature_names_out()

    # retrain seed=42 (the one Figures 2-3 came from) to get a live model for permutation importance
    model, _ = train_model(
        n_features, BEST_HIDDEN_SIZES, Z_train2, y_train2.values, Z_val, y_val.values,
        dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False, lr=LR, weight_decay=0.0,
        batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, patience=PATIENCE, seed=42,
    )
    test_pred = predict(model, Z_test)

    # --- subgroup errors ---
    meta = X_test.reset_index(drop=True).copy()
    meta["precipitation"] = meta.apply(precipitation_regime, axis=1)
    meta["abs_error"] = np.abs(y_test.values - test_pred)
    meta["actual"] = y_test.values
    meta["predicted"] = test_pred

    subgroup_rows = []
    for col in ["seasons", "precipitation", "holiday"]:
        for level, group in meta.groupby(col):
            subgroup_rows.append({
                "group_col": col, "level": level, "n": len(group),
                "mae": float(group["abs_error"].mean()),
            })
    subgroup_df = pd.DataFrame(subgroup_rows).sort_values("mae", ascending=False)
    print("--- Subgroup MAE (sorted, worst first) ---")
    print(subgroup_df.to_string(index=False))
    worst_subgroup = subgroup_df.iloc[0]

    # --- worst 10 examples ---
    worst = meta.sort_values("abs_error", ascending=False).head(10)
    worst_cols = ["seasons", "precipitation", "holiday", "hour", "temperature", "actual", "predicted", "abs_error"]
    print("\n--- 10 worst examples ---")
    print(worst[worst_cols].to_string(index=False))

    # --- permutation importance (manual: shuffle each preprocessed column, measure RMSE increase) ---
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    base_rmse = regression_metrics(y_test, test_pred)["rmse"]
    importances = {}
    for j, name in enumerate(feature_names):
        increases = []
        for _ in range(N_PERMUTATIONS):
            Z_perm = Z_test.copy()
            Z_perm[:, j] = rng.permutation(Z_perm[:, j])
            perm_pred = predict(model, Z_perm)
            perm_rmse = regression_metrics(y_test, perm_pred)["rmse"]
            increases.append(perm_rmse - base_rmse)
        importances[name] = float(np.mean(increases))

    importance_series = pd.Series(importances).sort_values(ascending=False)
    print("\n--- Permutation importance (RMSE increase when shuffled, top 10) ---")
    print(importance_series.head(10).to_string())

    with open(OUT_DIR / "step6_error_analysis.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({
            "subgroups": subgroup_df.to_dict(orient="records"),
            "worst_examples": worst[worst_cols].to_dict(orient="records"),
            "permutation_importance": importance_series.to_dict(),
            "base_test_rmse": base_rmse,
        }, f, indent=2, default=str)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Error per subgroup (test MAE, seed=42 model):

Subgroup n MAE Holiday 72 193.49 Summer 456 178.35 Rain 147 146.27 Spring 432 139.78 Autumn 384 130.13 Dry 1,472 129.42 No Holiday 1,632 124.30 Winter 432 58.13 Snow 85 56.37

Holiday hours are the single worst subgroup (MAE 193.49, 56% worse than non-holiday's 124.30) — and the EDA's own risk #3 predicted exactly this: only 72 test hours are holidays (and 14 training days), too few for the network to learn holiday-specific demand patterns distinctly from an ordinary day. Season follows the same demand-level logic as the subgroup error, not an inverted one: Summer (highest, most variable demand) is hardest to predict; Winter (lowest, flattest demand) is easiest — an MLP's absolute error naturally tracks the scale of what it's predicting. The same pattern explains precipitation: snow (MAE 56.37) is the easiest precipitation regime despite being a bad-weather outlier, because snow suppresses demand so reliably (EDA: median 149 bikes/h) that predicting "low" is almost always right; rain (MAE 146.27) is harder because rain's effect on demand is less consistent (some rainy commuter hours still see meaningful ridership).

Ten worst individual errors are dominated by one failure mode: Summer and Spring daytime hours with ordinary ("dry", mild temperature) conditions where the network over-predicted by 950-1,250 bikes — e.g., actual 477 vs. predicted 1,729 at 19h, 22.3°C, Spring. The common thread is that these are hours where the weather features alone suggest high demand (favorable temperature, no precipitation, daytime/evening), but something the model cannot see — a specific one-off event, a local disruption, or just the natural variance day-to-day beyond what 12 months of data can characterize — suppressed actual ridership. Two of the ten worst errors run the other way (under-prediction on unusually high-demand hours), consistent with Figure 3's funnel: both failure directions grow with the scale of predicted demand, not with any single feature.

Permutation importance (RMSE increase when a feature is shuffled, mean over 20 permutations):

Feature RMSE increase hour_sin 392.16 hour_cos 320.54 temperature 238.08 seasons_Summer 191.65 solar_radiation 166.36 seasons_Autumn 127.63 humidity 105.49

This matches the EDA almost exactly. The EDA's bivariate analysis ranked temperature (Spearman 0.617) and hour (0.423) as the two strongest single-feature correlates of demand — here, the cyclical encoding splits hour into hour_sin/hour_cos, and together they dwarf every other feature's importance, with temperature a clear third. The EDA data's 4 informative structure (season → precipitation → hour trajectories, its Figure 15) also shows up directly: seasons_Summer and solar_radiation (a precipitation/weather proxy) are next in line. The network did not discover some orthogonal driver the EDA missed — it learned, with more nuance (non-linear, interacting), the same two or three drivers the univariate and bivariate analysis already pointed at.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
Was the network worthwhile? Yes, relative to the mandatory bar: a 53.2% MAE reduction against Ridge is not a marginal win, and Figure 2/3 show the fit is genuinely tight, not an artifact of the metric. Relative to the optional Random Forest baseline, the picture is more honest: the network edges it out (131.55 vs. 133.77 MAE) but by less than the network's own seed-to-seed noise (± 3.07) — so "the network clearly beats the strongest baseline" would overstate this result. A fair summary is that the network matches a well-tuned Random Forest here, at a fraction of the parameter count, while requiring far more engineering (early stopping, an 8-configuration search, explicit target transform) to get there.

Limitations: (1) one year of data, so the model's validity for a different year's climate or a structurally different mix of holidays is untested — the EDA already flagged this. (2) Holiday hours remain the weakest subgroup by a wide margin, with only 72 test examples to judge that weakness on — not enough to be confident it generalizes past this particular test split. (3) The negative regularization result (Step 4) is itself a limitation of generality: it says this specific network, on this specific amount of data, did not need dropout/weight decay/batchnorm — not that regularization is never useful for this task; a larger network or less data would likely flip that conclusion.

Affected stakeholders: the bike-fleet operations team that would use these predictions for rebalancing. The error-analysis finding that Summer and holiday hours are the least reliable is directly actionable — operational buffers (extra bikes staged, more frequent rebalancing runs) should be largest exactly when the model is least trustworthy, not uniform across all hours.

Future work: multiple years of data to test the "only one year" limitation directly; an explicit holiday-type feature (which specific holiday, not just a binary flag) given how poorly the current 72-example signal generalizes; and testing whether the "regularization hurts" finding is specific to this network's small size by re-running the Step 4 search at the Random-Forest-matching capacity this network already reaches, to see whether regularization starts earning its keep once the network is made deliberately larger than necessary.

Item Value Dataset UCI Bank Marketing, older full version: bank-full.csv URL https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/222/bank%2Bmarketing Size (original) 45,211 rows x 17 columns (16 input features + target) Target y: did the client subscribe to a term deposit? Motivation. Direct-marketing calls are expensive, and only 11.70% of the contacted clients in this dataset subscribed. A classifier that ranks clients by their chance of subscribing before a call is made could help the bank prioritise calls. The dataset is real (a Portuguese bank, May 2008 to November 2010), well documented, and has a mix of numerical and categorical features and a clear binary target, so it fits a classification EDA.

First risk. The target is imbalanced (11.70% yes, ratio 7.55 : 1), and the strongest single input, duration, is target leakage: it is only known after the call. We exclude it (see 1B), so realistic predictive signal will be weaker than published benchmarks that use it. A second risk is that the file is chronological and the subscription rate drifts strongly over time (1B).

docs.title: 3A. Numerical x numerical
docs.text:
Choice: Spearman. 4 of the 6 numerical features are strongly skewed (balance, campaign, pdays, previous), and pdays/previous are dominated by a sentinel/zero mass. Pearson assumes linear relationships and is sensitive to extreme values, while Spearman uses ranks: it captures monotone relationships and is robust to outliers. Pearson is shown only for comparison.

Top pairs by |Spearman|:

pair spearman pearson pdays - previous 0.986 0.439 day - campaign 0.139 0.162 campaign - pdays -0.112 -0.089 campaign - previous -0.108 -0.031 age - balance 0.096 0.096 day - pdays -0.093 -0.093

Figure 6 - conclusion. - The only strongly correlated pair is pdays - previous: Spearman 0.986, compared with Pearson 0.439. Pearson understates it because the relationship is monotone but far from linear (a large sentinel mass plus long tails). - All other pairs have |rho| <= 0.139. The next strongest are day - campaign (0.139) and campaign - pdays (-0.112). Apart from the pair above, the numerical features are close to non-redundant.

Figure 7 - conclusion. The 0.986 correlation is driven almost entirely by the shared sentinel, since pdays = -1 exactly when previous = 0 (1B). Among previously contacted clients, Spearman is only -0.099 (Pearson -0.016), so the actual magnitudes are nearly unrelated. Redundancy: the two features duplicate the binary "previously contacted" information, not their values. Part 2 should encode that flag once and keep both magnitudes (or test dropping one) instead of treating them as collinear duplicates.

docs.title: 3B. Categorical x target
docs.text:
The training base rate is 11.70%. Rates for every level of every categorical feature, with 95% Wilson intervals and lift, are in part1_outputs/categorical_target_rates_train.csv. The spread between each feature's highest and lowest level rate:

feature max - min rate (pp) poutcome 55.4 month 44.2 job 21.6 contact 10.7 housing 9.0 education 6.3 default 5.9 loan 5.8 marital 5.0

The features with the largest spread are poutcome (55.4 pp), month (44.2 pp), job (21.6 pp). The smallest is marital (5.0 pp). The selected figures cover the strongest and most decision-relevant features.

Figure 8 - conclusion. - poutcome separates the classes most. Clients whose previous campaign was a success subscribe at 64.6%, against 12.3% (failure), 16.5% (other) and 9.2% (unknown = never contacted). - contact = unknown has a much lower rate (4.1%) than cellular (14.8%) and telephone (13.9%). This matches the early-period artifact found in 1B, so it partly encodes time. - Clients without a housing loan (16.7% vs 7.7%) or without a personal loan (12.6% vs 6.8%) subscribe more often. - The intervals for poutcome = success, contact = unknown, housing and loan do not overlap with their contrasts. cellular and telephone overlap, so the contact channel itself adds little once unknown is separated out.

Figure 9 - conclusion. Contact volume and subscription rate move in opposite directions (Spearman correlation across the 12 months: -0.87). - The busiest month has the lowest rate: may (6.7%, n = 11,062). - Low-volume months have rates above 30%: mar (50.9%, n = 391), sep (45.2%, n = 451), oct (43.8%, n = 592), dec (47.2%, n = 178). The maximum is mar (50.9%, n = 391). - Volume and rate are drawn as two panels on separate axes, not as a dual-axis chart. - month is strongly predictive, but given the drift found in 1B it likely mixes seasonality with the period of data collection (there is no year column). Its confidence intervals are wide for the thin months.

Figure 10 - conclusion. - job: students (28.9%) and retired clients (23.0%) subscribe far above the base rate. Blue-collar clients (7.3%), housemaids (8.4%), entrepreneurs (8.5%) and services workers (8.9%) subscribe below it. - education: the rate increases from primary (8.6%) to secondary (10.7%) to tertiary (14.9%). unknown (13.2%) has a wide interval, consistent with its small size. - These features carry moderate, roughly ordinal signal. job = unknown (12.0%) has a very wide interval and is too small to interpret.
